source.title: Representation Learning on a Random Lattice

record.tranche_reason: The paper's own random-lattice model predicts multidimensional component features, explicitly contrasting with the one-dimensional-feature assumption. This is a theoretical refinement, not an empirical test on trained networks.
record.gate_note: The paper derives predictions from a random-lattice/percolation model but reports no measurements on neural networks. Statements about SAE behavior and LLM features that are attributed to other studies are cited findings, not rows here.
record.test_reason: A purely theoretical paper with no neural-network experiments. It gives a specific argument, from a random-lattice/percolation model of data geometry, that component features should be multidimensional (about 4-D). This directly restates V6, so it counts as T5 by argument only.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors present a random-lattice/percolation model of data geometry that sorts features into context, component and surface types. They argue SAEs and superposition fit mainly the subcritical regime. They predict 4-D component features and possibly 1-D context features, and a hierarchical, power-law feature structure consistent with SAE feature splitting. All of this is framed as qualitative consistency with prior findings, not as new evidence.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a theoretical random-lattice and percolation model to derive feature-geometry predictions; it does not implement the original toy-network method.
record.method_sensitivity: Predictions vary with the percolation regime; the paper associates different feature prevalence with p ≲ pc, p ≳ pc, and p ≫ pc.

fits_no_version.finding: Table 1 and Section 3.4 argue that sparse, superposable features dominate only in the subcritical data regime (p ≲ pc). In supercritical regimes features are expected to be dense and compositional, so sparse dictionary learning may be less useful there.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Whether features are sparse and superposed (and SAE-recoverable) depends on the percolation regime of the data distribution.

record.problems: The claim-relevant conclusions are theoretical predictions from a stylized random-lattice model; the paper reports no neural-network experiments validating them.
record.rows_left_out: Cited results about LLM neurons, SAEs, feature splitting, and multidimensional features are not rows because this paper does not itself produce those results.

untested.parts: No toy networks are trained. Nearly orthogonal storage, the sparsity phase transition and regular geometry are not examined; superposition is only invoked as plausible for sparse context features.
Capacity competition and dedicated dimensions for important features are not addressed.
No alternative mechanism for polysemanticity is tested.
No measurements in LLMs. Neuron and SAE findings are cited from other work.
Concerns about SAE atomicity, feature splitting and hierarchy are drawn from cited work; nothing is tested here.
No empirical dimensionality estimate for any trained network. The 4-D prediction for component features is derived, not observed.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'challenges' label is too strong for a theory-only prediction that the author explicitly limits to one feature class; it is downgraded to 'limits_scope'. The paper is a preprint with no experiments. Cited empirical results (Engels et al., Bricken et al., Gurnee et al.) are correctly left out of the rows.

versions.untested_parts: The paper discusses sparsity-dependent conditions under which superposition may be useful, but does not test toy networks storing overlapping, nearly orthogonal directions or the claimed regular geometry.
It does not test competition for model capacity or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions.
It does not test whether polysemanticity arises through mechanisms other than capacity pressure.
It reports no new measurements of feature distribution across neurons or SAE recovery in LLMs; relevant examples are cited from other work.
It discusses concerns about SAE features and hierarchical structure, but does not itself test whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical.
The prediction concerns component features in the model; it does not establish dimensionality in trained networks or the dimensionality of all feature types.

rows.subject: random lattice model
rows.operation_detail: Theoretically predicts component-feature dimensionality from percolation-cluster geometry.

conditions.value: high-dimensional clusters near pc; d ≥ 6, s ≫ 1

rows.baseline: The one-dimensional-subspace assumption of the linear representation hypothesis
rows.value: Component features should generically require four-dimensional representations.
rows.note: This is a prediction of the paper's theoretical model, not an observed measurement in a trained network. The paper separately says context features need not be multidimensional.
rows.check: The value is a theoretical prediction from a stylized percolation model, not a measurement on any trained network. The 'reversed' state applies only to component features: the paper says context features need not be multidimensional, so the condition must stay restricted to component features.

relationships.reason: The model predicts component features need about 4-D representations, while context features may be 1-D (r1). This qualifies V6 by feature type, but it rests on theory alone with no network measurement, so it does not reach 'challenges'.
relationships.display_finding: The model predicts that component features need about 4-D representations while context features may be 1-D; this rests on theory alone, with no measurement in a trained network.
